lede: Write a vector as so far across and so far up, and every calculation splits into two small ones that never mix. That one idea carries the whole vectors question, including the five-mark part the Summer 2024 examiners found few candidates could get past the first mark of.
can: Add, subtract and scale vectors in i and j form without losing a sign.
Turn one vector equation into two scalar equations, and solve them.
Use position vectors, F = ma and the motion formulae in vector form.

md: A vector in $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ form is two numbers under one name: how far across and how far up. Adding two vectors means walking one and then the other, nose to tail. The single arrow from start to finish is the sum, and its components are the totals of the two columns: the $\mathbf{i}$ terms together, the $\mathbf{j}$ terms together. Subtracting works the same way, one column at a time.

stem: Two forces, $(7\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-3\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j})$ N, act on a body. Find their resultant.

steps.decision: The resultant is the sum of the forces. The sum written out with its brackets is the method mark.
Total each column on its own. Adding a negative component takes it away.
Put the two totals back together as one vector: the answer keeps its i and its j.

prompt: Two forces, $(5\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-8\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})$ N, act on a body. What is the $\mathbf{i}$ component of their resultant, in newtons?
explain: Total the $\mathbf{i}$ column on its own, as in step 2 of See it: $5 + (-8) = -3$. The $\mathbf{j}$ terms never enter it; they total 7 in their own column.

twin.prompt: Two forces, $(2\mathbf{i} - 9\mathbf{j})$ N and $(6\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j})$ N, act on a body. What is the $\mathbf{j}$ component of their resultant, in newtons?

caption: Tripling the arrow triples both components. Tripling only one swings the arrow round.

md:
Multiplying a vector by a number stretches the arrow, so every component is multiplied, sign included. Leave one alone and the arrow turns as well as stretching.

For a combination such as $3\mathbf{a} - 2\mathbf{b}$, scale each vector on its own line first, with brackets, then combine column by column. Subtracting a negative component adds to the total.

title: Why the scalar cannot skip a component
md: An arrow's direction is set by how far up it goes for each step across. Triple both and that rate stays the same, so the arrow only gets longer. Triple one alone and the rate changes, so the arrow points somewhere new.

steps.decision: The 3 multiplies both components, so $-3\mathbf{j}$ becomes $-9\mathbf{j}$.
The same for $\mathbf{b}$, on its own line, before anything is combined.
Subtract column by column. Taking away −4 adds 4, and that is where the sign most often goes.

prompt: $\mathbf{a} = (2\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})$ and $\mathbf{b} = (3\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})$. What is the $\mathbf{j}$ component of $2\mathbf{a} - 3\mathbf{b}$?
explain: Scale first, as in steps 1 and 2 of See it: $2\mathbf{a}$ has $-10\mathbf{j}$ and $3\mathbf{b}$ has $-12\mathbf{j}$. Then $-10 - (-12) = 2$: taking away a negative adds.

twin.prompt: $\mathbf{a} = (\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j})$ and $\mathbf{b} = (4\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})$. What is the $\mathbf{j}$ component of $3\mathbf{a} - 2\mathbf{b}$?

text: Why one vector equation is two

md: $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are at right angles, so no amount of $\mathbf{i}$ can ever make any $\mathbf{j}$: a step east never moves you north. That is why the columns never mix, and it has a second use. When two vectors are equal, their $\mathbf{i}$ parts must match and their $\mathbf{j}$ parts must match. One vector equation carries two ordinary equations, exactly enough for two unknowns.

stem: Show that if $a\mathbf{i} + b\mathbf{j} = c\mathbf{i} + d\mathbf{j}$, then $a = c$ and $b = d$.

steps.decision: Gather the $\mathbf{i}$ terms on the left and the $\mathbf{j}$ terms on the right.

steps.working: The left side points along the x-axis; the right side points along the y-axis
steps.decision: A number times $\mathbf{i}$ is an arrow across and a number times $\mathbf{j}$ is an arrow up, at right angles to it.
Two arrows at right angles can only be equal if neither goes anywhere: both have zero length.
Equal vectors: the $\mathbf{i}$ parts equal and the $\mathbf{j}$ parts equal. Two equations, one from each direction.

explain: The $\mathbf{i}$ parts are equated with each other and the $\mathbf{j}$ parts with each other, as in step 4 of See it: two equations, so $p = 7$ and $q = 5$.

optionNotes.why: One equation from everything mixes the directions; each direction gives its own.
The i part is paired with the j part here. Match i with i and j with j.
Adding everything into one equation mixes the two directions. They are at right angles, so each direction gives an equation of its own.
This pairs each number with the one next to it on the page, not with its own direction: i goes with i, and j with j.

md: The paper's five-mark part gives vectors with letters in them and an equation they satisfy. The route never changes: substitute with a bracket round every vector, expand every bracket, then write one line for the $\mathbf{i}$ terms and one for the $\mathbf{j}$ terms. Drop the $\mathbf{i}$ and the $\mathbf{j}$ at that point; what is left is a pair of simultaneous equations.

title: Summer 2024 and 2025, Question 2(i)
md: Most candidates substituted and then stopped: few equated the $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ coefficients, and many left $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ inside their equations. In 2025 the sign of $-3 \times -3x$ was the slip.

stem: Forces $\mathbf{P} = (x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j})$ N and $\mathbf{Q} = (2y\mathbf{i} - x\mathbf{j})$ N satisfy $4\mathbf{P} - 3\mathbf{Q} = (32\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j})$ N. Find $x$ and $y$.

steps.decision: Substitute with a bracket round each vector, so the 4 and the $-3$ reach every term.
Expand. $-3 \times -x\mathbf{j}$ is $+3x\mathbf{j}$: two negatives make a plus.
Gather the $\mathbf{i}$ terms and equate them. The $\mathbf{i}$ has done its job and is dropped.
The same for the $\mathbf{j}$ terms: two ordinary equations, no $\mathbf{i}$ or $\mathbf{j}$ in either.
Eliminate, solve, then check both values in the equation you did not use: $3(5) + 4(-2) = 7$.

title: Vectors Using i and j notation
why: The same arithmetic at a slower pace, with every bracket written out. Watch the i line and the j line being kept apart.

prompt: $(x\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}) - 2(\mathbf{i} - y\mathbf{j}) = 5\mathbf{i} + 13\mathbf{j}$. What is the value of $y$?
explain: Expand first, as in step 2 of See it: $-2 \times -y\mathbf{j} = +2y\mathbf{j}$. The $\mathbf{j}$ line is $3 + 2y = 13$, so $y = 5$. Writing $-2y$ would give $-5$.

twin.prompt: $(4\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j}) - 3(x\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}) = -5\mathbf{i} + 10\mathbf{j}$. What is the value of $y$?

md: A position vector runs from the origin $O$ to a point: $\mathbf{a}$ is $\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ is $\overrightarrow{OB}$. The displacement from $A$ to $B$ is the arrow straight between them. Going there directly, or going round by $O$, ends in the same place, and that one fact gives the rule.

stem: Show that the displacement from $A$ to $B$ is $\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}$.

steps.decision: From $O$, going to $A$ and then on to $B$ lands where going straight to $B$ does.
The two arrows from $O$ are the position vectors.
Take $\mathbf{a}$ from both sides: the finish's position vector minus the start's.

prompt: $P$ has position vector $\mathbf{p}$ and $Q$ has position vector $\mathbf{q}$. What is $\overrightarrow{QP}$, the displacement from $Q$ to $P$?
explain: The journey starts at $Q$ and finishes at $P$, so it is the finish minus the start, as step 3 of See it shows.

twin.prompt: $C$ has position vector $\mathbf{c}$ and $D$ has position vector $\mathbf{d}$. What is $\overrightarrow{CD}$?
twin.explain: From $C$ to $D$: the finish, $\mathbf{d}$, minus the start, $\mathbf{c}$.

optionNotes.why: That is the journey from D back to C. The finish comes first.
Adding position vectors lands somewhere else entirely; the displacement is a difference.
That is the journey from P to Q: the same arrow, pointing back the other way.
Adding the position vectors lands at a point that is neither P nor Q. A displacement between two points takes one from the other.

text: Displacement and distance between two points

md: With numbers in, find $\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}$ one column at a time, with a bracket round each position vector so the minus reaches both components. That answer is a vector. If the question asks how far apart the points are, the distance is its magnitude, a single number, found as in the magnitude topic.

stem: $P$ has position vector $(-3\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ m and $Q$ has position vector $(5\mathbf{i} - 10\mathbf{j})$ m. Find $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and the distance $PQ$.

steps.decision: Finish minus start, with a bracket round each.
$5 - (-3) = 8$ and $-10 - 5 = -15$. This part asks for a vector, so both components stay.
A distance is a length: the magnitude of the displacement. Squaring removes the minus sign.

prompt: $A$ has position vector $(3\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})$ m and $B$ has position vector $(-2\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j})$ m. What is the $\mathbf{j}$ component of $\overrightarrow{AB}$, in metres?
explain: Finish minus start, one column at a time, as in step 2 of See it: $8 - (-4) = 12$. Taking away −4 adds 4; $-4 - 8 = -12$ would be the journey back.

twin.prompt: $C$ has position vector $(-\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ m and $D$ has position vector $(5\mathbf{i} - 7\mathbf{j})$ m. What is the $\mathbf{i}$ component of $\overrightarrow{CD}$, in metres?

md: $\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t$ and $\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{u}t + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$ work exactly as they do with numbers, one component at a time. The mass and the time stay plain numbers: dividing a force vector by the mass divides both of its components, and $t^2$ multiplies both components of $\mathbf{a}$.

stem: A particle of mass 2 kg has initial velocity $(4\mathbf{i} - 7\mathbf{j})$ m/s. A constant force $(6\mathbf{i} + 10\mathbf{j})$ N acts on it. Find its acceleration, then its displacement after 2 seconds.

steps.decision: $\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$ with the numbers in: this line earns the method mark.
Divide both components by the mass.
$\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{u}t + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$ with $t = 2$; square the time before it multiplies.
Work each term out, then add the columns.

prompt: A particle has initial velocity $(\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})$ m/s and constant acceleration $(2\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})$ m/s². What is the $\mathbf{j}$ component of its displacement after 3 seconds, in metres?
explain: As in steps 3 and 4 of See it, in the $\mathbf{j}$ column: $3 \times 3 + \tfrac{1}{2} \times (-4) \times 3^2 = 9 - 18 = -9$. Leaving $t$ unsquared gives 3.

twin.prompt: A particle has initial velocity $(-2\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j})$ m/s and constant acceleration $(6\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ m/s². What is the $\mathbf{i}$ component of its displacement after 2 seconds, in metres?

md: Read the last words of the part before you start. *In vector form*, *the resultant*, *the velocity* and *the displacement vector* all want an answer with $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ in it. *The magnitude*, *the speed* and *the distance* want one number. Giving one where the other was asked costs the marks: the Summer 2023 and Summer 2019 reports both saw it.

stem: A particle has velocity $(-9\mathbf{i} + 40\mathbf{j})$ m/s. Part (a) asks for its velocity in vector form; part (b) asks for its speed.

steps.decision: *In vector form*: both components stay, because the direction is part of the answer.
*Speed*: one number, the magnitude of the velocity. The minus sign goes when the component is squared.
A magnitude is longer than either component and shorter than their total, so 41 is believable.

prompt: Which of these parts wants a single number, not an answer in $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$?
options: Calculate the speed of the particle.
Find the velocity of the particle.
answer: Calculate the speed of the particle.
explain: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity, one number, as step 2 of See it found. A velocity and a displacement vector keep both components.

twin.prompt: Which of these parts wants an answer in $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$?
options: Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force.
twin.explain: A resultant force is a vector, so it keeps both components. A magnitude and a distance are single numbers.

optionNotes.option: Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force.
optionNotes.why: A magnitude is the size alone, one number, so it drops the i and the j.
A distance is a length, one number: the magnitude of the displacement, not the displacement itself.

optionNotes.option: Find the velocity of the particle.
optionNotes.why: A velocity has a direction, so it is written with both components; the speed is its size alone.
The word vector is in the question: it keeps its i and j. The distance OP would be the single number.

md: **A magnitude given, an unknown inside** (Summer 2021 paper). Build the resultant with the letter still in it, then set the sum of the squares of its components equal to the magnitude squared. The square root has two signs, so there are two answers.

**A missing force** (Summer 2023). Three forces add to $\mathbf{F}$ and two are given: the third is $\mathbf{F}$ minus the other two, a bracket round each. The report found the signs going astray in exactly this part.
**A number on the right too** (Summer 2024). The equation read $2\mathbf{a} - 3\mathbf{b} = 4\mathbf{c}$: multiply $\mathbf{c}$ by 4 before equating, or both equations are out by that factor.
**Speed, not velocity** (Summer 2019). A velocity from u + at came first, then its speed: the word in bold asked for one number, and most candidates stopped at the vector.

stem: Two forces, $(x\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})$ N and $(4\mathbf{i} - 15\mathbf{j})$ N, have a resultant of magnitude 13 N. Find the two possible values of $x$.

steps.decision: Build the resultant first, column by column; the letter stays inside the $\mathbf{i}$ component.
The magnitude squared is the sum of the squares of the components.
Move the known square across.
A square root has two signs, and both give a resultant 13 N long, as the figure shows.

prompt: Two forces, $(x\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ N and $(3\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ N, have a resultant of magnitude 5 N. What are the possible values of $x$?
explain: The resultant is $(x + 3)\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}$, so $(x + 3)^2 + 16 = 25$ and $x + 3 = \pm 3$, as in step 4 of See it: $x = 0$ or $x = -6$.

twin.prompt: Two forces, $(x\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})$ N and $(2\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j})$ N, have a resultant of magnitude 10 N. What are the possible values of $x$?

optionNotes.why: x + 2 = −6 works as well: the root has two signs, and both resultants are 10 N long.
That adds the sizes of the components to make 10. The magnitude squares them first.
The square root has two signs. x + 3 = −3 also gives a resultant 5 N long, pointing the other way across.
That adds the components to make 5. A magnitude squares, adds and roots them: (x + 3)² + 4² = 5².

stem: The force $\mathbf{F} = (2\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})$ N is the resultant of three forces. Two of them are $(6\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j})$ N and $(-3\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j})$ N. Find the third force.

steps.decision: The three forces add to $\mathbf{F}$, so the missing one is $\mathbf{F}$ minus the other two, each in its bracket.
Taking away −3 adds 3, and taking away −8 adds 8.

prompt: $(4\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})$ N is the resultant of three forces. Two of them are $(7\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-5\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j})$ N. What is the $\mathbf{j}$ component of the third force, in newtons?
explain: The resultant minus the other two, in the $\mathbf{j}$ column, as in step 2 of See it: $3 - (-2) - 6 = -1$.

twin.prompt: $(-2\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j})$ N is the resultant of three forces. Two of them are $(3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})$ N. What is the $\mathbf{i}$ component of the third force, in newtons?

md: A question can ask when a body is moving parallel to $\mathbf{i}$, or to $\mathbf{j}$. Parallel to $\mathbf{i}$ means the velocity has no $\mathbf{j}$ component at all. Write the velocity with $t$ left as a letter, set the $\mathbf{j}$ component to zero and solve: one component, one equation. No CCEA paper has asked it yet, but it uses nothing new.

stem: A particle has initial velocity $(3\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j})$ m/s and constant acceleration $(\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ m/s². When is it moving parallel to $\mathbf{i}$, and at what speed?

steps.decision: $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t$ with $t$ kept as a letter, so each component is an expression in $t$.
Parallel to $\mathbf{i}$: the $\mathbf{j}$ component is zero.
With no $\mathbf{j}$ part left, the speed is just the $\mathbf{i}$ component.

prompt: A particle has initial velocity $(-4\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ m/s and constant acceleration $(2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j})$ m/s². After how many seconds is it moving parallel to $\mathbf{j}$?
explain: Parallel to $\mathbf{j}$ means no $\mathbf{i}$ component: $-4 + 2t = 0$, so $t = 2$. This is step 2 of See it with the other component.

twin.prompt: A particle has initial velocity $(6\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})$ m/s and constant acceleration $(-3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j})$ m/s². After how many seconds is it moving parallel to $\mathbf{i}$?

md:
Add, subtract and scale vectors column by column, a bracket round every vector.
Equate the $\mathbf{i}$ parts and the $\mathbf{j}$ parts: one vector equation is two.
Find a displacement as the finish's position vector minus the start's.
Use $\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$ and the motion formulae one component at a time.
Keep $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ for a vector answer; give one number for a speed or a distance.

Vectors open the paper, as Question 1 or 2: five marks for unknowns in a vector equation, then a magnitude and a direction (Summer 2024 and 2025), or 2 + 2 + 2 on an acceleration, a displacement and a missing force (Summer 2023). The first mark is the substitution with brackets. Stuck? Expand, then one line for $\mathbf{i}$ and one for $\mathbf{j}$.
